findings.stemStart: Wine names won formal recognition as a species
findings.problem: The stem says 'a world trade agreement' and the key read 'The TRIPS agreement of the World Trade Organization', so it could be answered from the stem's own words. The longest distractor gave its own date (1957), which the stem's 1994 rules out. Bretton Woods was not an intellectual property instrument at all. The exp said TRIPS is why a producer elsewhere 'can still be stopped' from using a European name, which skips the Article 24 exceptions for prior use and names generic in a country.
findings.fix: Options are now four bare names with no hints: The TRIPS agreement, The Treaty of Rome, The Madrid Protocol, The Lisbon Agreement. Lisbon is a real appellation treaty, but it is WIPO's and dates from 1958. The key is unchanged. The exp now says what TRIPS obliges, that Lisbon binds only the states that joined it, and that TRIPS's exceptions are why bilateral wine agreements were still needed.
findings.source: TRIPS Agreement (Marrakesh, 1994), Articles 22 to 24; Lisbon Agreement for the Protection of Appellations of Origin (1958)

findings.stemStart: Until the reform that took effect in 2009,
findings.problem: The exp said wine and food GIs fell under 'one regulation' from 2024. Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 unified registration and protection, but the definitions and specification rules for wine GIs are still in the CMO Regulation 1308/2013.
findings.fix: Now: 'since 2024, one regulation governing how the names are registered and protected'.

findings.stemStart: Vin de pays was the French name for
findings.problem: Two distractors were not real categories. 'Vin de Qualite Superieure' is a mangled VDQS and 'Vin de Table Regional' never existed, but the house standard needs four real options. The obvious confusion, Vin de France, was missing. The exp also said 'the same zones', although several vins de pays were merged or renamed when they became IGPs.
findings.fix: Those two distractors are now Vin de France and Vin de Table, both real tiers. The key is unchanged. The exp now says 'broadly the same zones and rules', notes that the old table-wine tier became Vin de France, and that vin de pays survives as a protected traditional term, so a label can still carry the older wording.
findings.source: EU 2008/2009 wine CMO reform and the French move from vin de pays to IGP and from vin de table to Vin de France (2009 to 2011); vin de pays registered as a traditional term for French PGI wines

findings.stemStart: European law will not let a bottle print
findings.problem: The stem says American federal law 'asks for less than' eighty-five percent. Two distractors, 'Ninety percent' and 'The same eighty-five percent that Europe asks', were ruled out by the stem's own words, leaving a choice of two. The exp also said 'several' states set higher varietal minimums. Oregon is the only well-known one.
findings.fix: The two distractors are now 'Eighty percent of the wine' and 'Two-thirds of the wine', so all four figures sit under eighty-five. The key is unchanged. The exp now says the federal floor was fifty-one percent until the early 1980s, which explains that distractor. It also says 'a state may hold its own growers above the federal figure', which drops the unsupported 'several do'.
findings.source: 27 CFR 4.23 (75 percent varietal minimum, in force from 1 January 1983; 51 percent before); Oregon's state rule is the familiar stricter case

findings.stemStart: Set the French, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese systems
findings.problem: The exp said the neighbours adopted the French model 'long before any European harmonisation existed'. Italy's DOC law of 1963 came after the EEC's first wine market regulation (1962). Portugal's framework law of 1985 came after the Community's quality-wine rules of 1970.
findings.fix: Now: 'each in a national law of its own before the European categories applied to it', which is true of all three.
findings.source: Italian DPR 930/1963; EEC Regulation 24/1962 and Regulation 817/70; Portuguese Lei 8/85; Spanish Estatuto del Vino 1932

findings.problem: The exp made warming the whole cause of the growers' vineyard hierarchies from the 1990s ('That pressure is why...'). The VDP's classification also answered an older complaint: the 1971 must-weight ladder, with its blurred site names, said nothing about the vineyard.
findings.fix: Now: 'That pressure, added to an older complaint that the ladder said nothing about the site, helped push growers' associations to build vineyard hierarchies...'. The 2021 pyramid sentence is kept.
findings.source: German Wine Law 1971 and its 2021 reform; the history of the VDP classification

findings.problem: The exp gave 'pouring alongside rather than after' as a way round the problem. That makes no sense here: the wine is already poured alongside, and the cold spoonful still comes before each sip.

findings.stemStart: A tinny, almost metallic taste comes up the
findings.problem: The exp said lean white fish 'does not produce it at all', so the fault 'belongs to the oil'. That is too absolute. The off-taste is linked to iron in the wine oxidising fish lipids, and it has been shown with lean seafood as well. Oily fish make it far worse, not uniquely possible.
findings.fix: Now: 'Lean white fish produces far less of it, which is why the oily species are the ones to keep a tannic red away from.' The key is unchanged.
findings.source: Tamura et al., J. Agric. Food Chem. 2009 (iron in wine and the fishy aftertaste with seafood); standard pairing teaching on oily fish and tannic reds
